name: Lyonnais Francoprovençal, St. Martin-en-Haut
catalog_citation: Kasstan, Jonathan Richard. 2015. Lyonnais (Francoprovençal). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 45(3) (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100315000250
catalog_locator: p. 353, section 'Stress' (also p. 352-353 'Vowels' on preserved unstressed final vowels)
catalog_quote: Stress. Owing to the fact that Francoprovençal retains a number of Latin atonic vowels, the stress pattern can vary and can fall on either paroxytonic or oxytonic syllables (compare cela [səˈla] ‘that’ and sela [ˈsøla] ‘chair’). As with the Occitan varieties, this feature differentiates these Lyonnais varieties of Francoprovençal markedly from SF. ... Francoprovençal preserves a number of unstressed final vowels. For example, unstressed Latin atonic A is maintained as /a/, e.g. TABULAM > trâbla [ˈtʁɔbla] ‘table’, which also undergoes raising to [i] when preceded by a palatal, e.g. VACCAM > vache [ˈvaʃi] ‘cow’. ... Despite the variability in final vowels present in Francoprovençal, there is often a reduced vocalic quality in connected speech, and so schwa is also common in unstressed syllables.
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for fran1260: Nagy 2000 'Stress and schwa in Faetar' (Benjamins, CILT 212, pp. 238-254; Benjamins page could not be reached by automated download, Crossref shows no OA link). An open author's HTML version was found on Nagy's own site (ngn.artsci.utoronto.ca/zip/stress.schwa.zip), downloaded, unzipped and read in full; the reference was attached to fran1260 only by Glottolog's computerized assignment from the word 'faetar'), so relevance is another language or variety. Its finding (stress lexically marked, on the rightmost non-schwa vowel within the last three syllables, open or closed) and its second-hand statement on Gallic Francoprovençal (lexically marked within the last two syllables, minimal pair ['tsata] ~ [tsa'ta], Martin 1990:673) are consistent with the catalog's lexical coding for Lyonnais (Kasstan 2015) and with Stich 2001 already held by the project; nothing contradicts. It does not supersede Kasstan 2015, which describes the exact catalog variety. Nothing remains unread for this item; the Glottolog tagging error (Faetar -> fran1260 rather than faet1240) is worth noting in the per-language bibliography. Nagy's CV also lists 'Nagy 2000. Faetar. Munich: Lincom Europa (LW/M 299)', a descriptive grammar of Faetar (not open; abstract page saved), relevant only to faet1240.

new_statements.quote: Stress always appears on the rightmost non-schwa vowel of a word. The stressed syllable is always one of the last three syllables in the word. However, stress is not on a fixed syllable, counting from the left or from the right, nor is it consistently on either an odd or an even syllable. Furthermore, stress may be on either an open or closed syllable [...] Historical evidence also supports lexically marked stress, as Francoprovençal, the source language of Faetar, has lexically marked stress. Although Francoprovençal requires that stress be on one of the last two syllables, there are minimal pairs like ['†ata] 'sing, 2nd sg. imperative' vs. [†a'ta] 'sing, 2nd pl. imperative' (Martin 1990:673).

new_statements.reading: Lexically marked (unpredictable) word stress within a right-edge window: last three syllables in Faetar (faet1240), last two syllables in Gallic Francoprovençal (second-hand via Martin 1990 LRL). Consistent with the catalog's lexical coding, but the first-hand part concerns Faetar, a sister language, not the Lyonnais variety the catalog record describes.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Cambridge Core PDF we hold of Kasstan 2015 at p. 353 'Stress' (and p. 352-353 'Vowels'), locator correct; only cosmetic issues (segment order, added period after heading). (2) Deciding source: a 2015 JIPA Illustration of the exact variety, i.e. a peer-reviewed phonetic description, not pedagogical or second-hand; the near-minimal pair cela [səˈla] vs sela [ˈsøla] (both CV.CV, both final [a]) justifies lexical within a right-edge two-syllable window rather than a weight/final-vowel rule. (3) Independent confirmation downloaded now: Stich 2001 (Paris V thesis, open) states for Francoprovençal generally that stress falls on one of the last two syllables and that the oxytone/paroxytone opposition is phonemic (tsantâ 'chanter' ~ tsanta 'chante!'), matching our classification; its caveat that north-western 'francoprovençal dégradé'
